name: Change of the weak letters (iʿlāl)
definition: The changes that wāw, yāʾ and alif (and hamza) undergo in a word for ease of speech: turned into another letter, made silent, or dropped.
body: Iʿlāl has three kinds. By change (qalb) a weak letter becomes another: the wāw of the root w-z-n becomes yāʾ in mīzān, whose underlying form is miwzān. By making silent (taskīn or naql) a weak letter loses its vowel to the letter before it: yaqūlu from an underlying yaqwulu. By dropping (ḥadhf) it falls away: the wāw of waʿada in yaʿidu and ʿid.

The books of ṣarf give most of their pages to these rules, in the chapters on the mithāl, the ajwaf, the nāqiṣ and the lafīf: Marāḥ al-arwāḥ has a chapter for each, and al-Shāfiya and al-Mumtiʿ set out the rules with their conditions and exceptions. Where a form keeps its weak letter against the rule it is called shādhdh.

examples.text: miwzān becomes mīzān: the wāw after a kasra turns to yāʾ (Marāḥ al-arwāḥ).
waʿada, yaʿidu, ʿid: the wāw drops in the present and the imperative.
